Key Research Thinking Patterns: Quantitative Biomarker Derivation from Bilateral Asymmetry: Developing computer-aided detection schemes that extract quantitative image markers from bilateral mammographic density asymmetry to predict the risk of mammography-occult tumors, specifically identifying BIRADS 2 patients who require adjunct MRI screening.

Computational Enhancement of Optical Resolution: Utilizing Fourier ptychography microscopy (FPM) with phase retrieval algorithms and multi-angle LED illumination to synthesize high numerical aperture (NA) imaging, achieving resolution comparable to 100x oil immersion lenses while maintaining a wide field of view for automated chromosome karyotyping.

Multi-View Contextual Modeling via Transformers: Employing Multi-view Vision Transformers (MVT) with local and global attention mechanisms to capture inter-mammogram dependencies in unregistered multi-view mammograms, thereby improving benign vs. malignant mass classification accuracy over single-view CNNs.

Robustness-Driven Semi-Supervised Learning: Integrating Virtual Adversarial Training (VAT) into convolutional neural networks to leverage unlabeled data and enhance model robustness against perturbations, improving diagnostic accuracy in scenarios with limited labeled medical image datasets.
Summary Description: Liu Hong is a biomedical engineer specializing in computational imaging, machine learning, and medical image analysis. Her research focuses on two primary translational goals: enhancing breast cancer screening through computer-aided detection (CAD) and advancing automated cytogenetic analysis for leukemia diagnosis. In breast imaging, she develops quantitative risk markers based on bilateral mammographic density asymmetry and utilizes Multi-view Vision Transformers to improve the classification of benign and malignant masses from multi-view mammograms. In cytogenetics, she pioneers the application of Fourier ptychography microscopy (FPM) to achieve high-resolution, wide-field chromosome karyotyping, overcoming the field-of-view limitations of conventional high-magnification microscopy. Her methodological expertise includes semi-supervised learning with Virtual Adversarial Training, phase retrieval algorithms, and deep learning architectures designed for robustness in limited-data clinical settings. Her work bridges advanced optical physics and data-driven AI to create high-throughput, accurate diagnostic tools for clinical radiology and hematology.
